adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Saltmarsh Restoration Log — Blackwater Reserve, 2016 to 2021

When the reserve was established in the late 1980s, the southern marsh was grazed by cattle and drained by a network of straight channels dug in the previous century. By the time the restoration team surveyed the site in March 2016, the drainage had lowered the water table enough that brackish water pushed inland on every spring tide, killing the reed beds that once supported bitterns and marsh harriers. The survey report, which ran to more than two hundred pages, recommended blocking the channels, removing the sea wall in three places, and reintroducing tidal flow gradually over five years rather than all at once.

The first phase began that autumn. Contractors brought in heavy plant along a temporary track laid across the northern field, and the noise drove the breeding waders off the reserve for two seasons. Volunteers planted around nine thousand cordgrass plugs by hand, usually in cold drizzle, and the warden kept a daily count of birds and water levels in a notebook that later became the backbone of the monitoring record. The project was funded by a combination of the county council, a national lottery grant and a charitable trust set up by a local birdwatcher who had been visiting the site since the 1970s.

Not every intervention worked. The first attempt to remove the sea wall in the eastern corner was abandoned after a storm took away the temporary access road, and the contractors had to wait until the following summer for a calm enough tide window. Two of the sluice gates seized within months of installation and were replaced under warranty. A trial planting of eelgrass failed completely in the first year, probably because the sediment was still too anoxic, and the team decided to wait rather than try again immediately.

By the second summer, however, the shallow bays, which for decades had been covered with a thick mat of green algae each spring, were clear enough to see the gravel bottom. Fish returned first, then the invertebrates that feed on them, and by 2019 the first otter spraints in twenty years were recorded on the southern bank. The reed beds recovered more slowly; the warden estimated that they had regained perhaps a third of their former extent by the end of the project.

The volunteer programme grew alongside the science. A rota of around forty people, most of them retired, took turns to count wildfowl at dawn and to pick up litter along the new footpaths. The warden trained them in a single afternoon each autumn, handed out laminated identification sheets, and gave them the hide keys. Their records, though less rigorous than the professional surveys, closed gaps in the data that the paid team could never have covered, and two of the volunteers went on to publish a short paper on the return of bearded tits to the eastern reed bed.

The final report, published in November 2021, concluded that the site had met four of its five targets. Water quality had improved sharply, bird numbers had risen, and the public footpath along the seawall now carried more than forty thousand visitors a year. The fifth target, a self-sustaining population of breeding avocets, was not met, though a pair nested unsuccessfully in the spring of 2020 and the team expected them to return.

Lessons recorded for other projects were mostly about patience: allow a full tidal cycle before judging a change, keep the monitoring simple enough that a small team can maintain it, and expect at least one major intervention to fail for reasons nobody predicted.
